documents.verification: NASA Technical Standards System summary page for NASA-STD-3001_VOL_1, read 2026-08-18, states Version C, Document Date 09/15/2023, Is Active? ACTIVE. The downloaded PDF's cover page states 'Approved: 2023-09-15' and 'Superseding NASA-STD-3001, Volume 1, Revision B'.
documents.rationale: Added beyond the Volume 2 originally specified, because Volume 2 does not contain the standard's fatigue requirements. Scanning all 1,579 of its requirements found 51 mentioning sleep, fatigue or workload and none stating a work-rest limit; Volume 1 section 6.1 is titled 'Circadian Shifting Operations and Fatigue Management' and [V1 4014] states the work-hours limit requirement. Omitting it would have meant compiling an authoritative fatigue corpus from the one volume of the standard that has no fatigue requirements in it.

documents.title: Evidence Report: Risk of Performance Decrements and Adverse Health Outcomes Resulting from Sleep Loss, Circadian Desynchronization, and Work Overload
documents.verification: NTRS record 20160003864, read 2026-08-18: distribution PUBLIC, copyright PUBLIC_USE_PERMITTED, status CURATED, publication date 2016-01-01, report number JSC-CN-35774. NTRS also holds an earlier issue of the same Evidence Report as 20150016964 (2015, JSC-CN-34196, one additional author); the 2016 issue is the later of the two and the one ingested. A search of NTRS for this risk title returned no issue later than 2016.
documents.rationale: NASA's own evidence base for exactly the risk HAVEN scores: sleep loss, circadian desynchronization and work overload as causes of crew performance decrement. It is why the deterministic tier models homeostatic pressure, circadian phase and workload at all, and it is the document a reviewer would open to challenge that modelling. Chosen over the individual studies it summarises because one review with NASA's own risk framing is worth more here than five primary papers.

documents.title: Crew Factors in Flight Operations IX: Effects of Planned Cockpit Rest on Crew Performance and Alertness in Long-Haul Operations
documents.verification: NTRS record 19950006379, read 2026-08-18: distribution PUBLIC, copyright GOV_PUBLIC_USE_PERMITTED, status CURATED, publication date 1994-09-01, report numbers NASA-TM-108839 / DOT-FAA-92-24 / A-94134. A final technical memorandum with no later revision in NTRS.
documents.rationale: The measurement behind HAVEN's short_rest_then_proceed action. Rosekind et al. gave one group a planned 40-minute rest in cruise and measured the effect on EEG sleep, psychomotor vigilance and physiological alertness against a no-rest control. HAVEN's forward projection claims a protected rest raises predicted alertness; this is the study that says whether a planned rest of that order does anything, and it is the right document to cite when somebody asks where the claim comes from.

documents.rationale: The operational countermeasure taxonomy HAVEN's action types map onto: preventive strategies taken before duty, and operational strategies taken during it. HAVEN can recommend a second operator, a short rest, a rotation or a deferral, and this is the NASA document that says what such countermeasures are for and what they do not fix. Included over the broader Fatigue Countermeasures Program literature because it is the one that states the strategies operationally rather than reporting a single experiment.
